items.text: CRITICAL THINKING

items.label: section_header
items.text: Metals:

items.label: list_item
items.text: tend to be solids withhigh melting and boiling points, and with relatively high densities (but as with several of the properties in this list, there are exceptions, for example mercury is a liquid)

items.label: list_item
items.text: are shiny (have a metallic lustre) when they are polished or freshly cut

items.label: list_item
items.text: are malleable (can be hammered into shape)

items.label: list_item
items.text: are ductile (can be drawn into wires)

items.label: list_item
items.text: are good conductors of electricity and heat

items.label: list_item
items.text: form ionic compounds (see Chapter 7)

items.label: list_item
items.text: form positive ions in their compounds (see Chapter 7).

items.label: section_header
items.text: Non-metals:

items.label: list_item
items.text: tend to have low melting and boiling points (there are some exceptions, e.g. carbon and silicon)

items.label: list_item
items.text: tend to be brittle when they are solids

items.label: list_item
items.text: don't have the same type of shine as metals

items.label: list_item
items.text: don't usually conduct electricity; carbon (in the form of graphite) and silicon are again exceptions

items.label: list_item
items.text: are poor conductors of heat (diamond is an exception; it is the best conductor of heat of all the elements)

items.label: list_item
items.text: form both ionic and covalent compounds (see Chapters 7 and 8)

items.label: list_item
items.text: tend to form negative ions in ionic compounds (see Chapter 7).
